steps.say: Weight loss surgery is offered by numbers, not by appearance. A body mass index over 40 qualifies on its own, while over 35 needs an additional disease such as diabetes or sleep apnoea. Over 30 qualifies when type 2 diabetes stays uncontrolled despite medicines. No one is listed without a team review by dietitians, psychologists and anaesthetists.
steps.tx: **Metabolic surgery** (weight-loss operations improving diabetes) suits a **body mass index** (weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared) above **40** alone, above **35** when sleep apnoea, hypertension or diabetes coexists, and above **30** when type 2 diabetes defies medicines. Booking follows **multidisciplinary assessment** (combined review by dietetics, psychology and anaesthesia).

steps.say: The sleeve turns the stomach into a narrow banana by removing the stretchy outer three quarters. Calibration is done over a bougie, a sizing tube between 36 and 40 French, so every surgeon makes the same tube. The outlet valve is left intact, which keeps ulcers rare, but one patient in five gets worse reflux from the high pressure tube.
steps.tx: **Sleeve gastrectomy** (converting the stomach into a slim banana tube) removes **75 to 80** percent of gastric volume, calibrated over a **36 to 40** French **bougie** (sizing tube inside the lumen). Keeping the pylorus (outlet valve) holds ulcers down compared with bypass, yet **20** percent suffer worse reflux as the tight sleeve drives pressure up.

steps.say: The Roux-en-Y builds a tiny egg cup pouch and joins the small bowel to it in a Y shape. The food limb measures 75 to 150 cm and the bile limb 50 cm, and remission comes mainly from rerouting and gut hormones rather than the lengths alone. Reflux is cured because no acid pool remains, but the rearranged bowel leaves gaps where internal hernias form and the new join can ulcerate.
steps.tx: **Roux-en-Y gastric bypass** (small pouch joined to mid small bowel in a Y) builds a **30** mL pouch with **75 to 150** cm **alimentary limb** (food-carrying segment) and a **50** cm biliopancreatic limb (bile-carrying segment). Diabetes remission and reflux control beat the sleeve, at the cost of **internal hernia** (bowel slipping through mesenteric gaps) and marginal ulcer risk.

steps.say: The one anastomosis bypass is the simpler cousin with a single join instead of two. A long 200 cm bile limb is brought up to the pouch, which gives strong diabetes control with a shorter operation. The price is bile washing back into the pouch and stronger malabsorption, so these patients are watched closely for reflux and vitamin shortfalls.
steps.tx: **One-anastomosis gastric bypass** (single-join bypass with a long bile limb) uses a **200** cm biliopancreatic limb with one gastrojejunostomy (stomach-to-bowel join). Weight and diabetes results match the classic bypass with a shorter operation, but **bile reflux** (alkaline washback into the pouch) and malabsorption need surveillance with endoscopy and bloods.

steps.say: A leak in the first week is the emergency every bariatric unit fears. The pulse races above 120, fever sets in, and pain is felt in the shoulder from diaphragmatic irritation. There is no role for waiting, the patient is returned to theatre for washout and drainage. A stricture is the opposite story weeks later, with gradually worsening dysphagia that is stretched open endoscopically.
steps.tx: An early **staple-line leak** (failed seal along the cut edge) declares itself inside **7** days through pulse above **120**, fever and shoulder-tip pain, demanding emergency washout with drainage. Later **strictures** (scarred narrow joins) emerge at **3 to 6** weeks with worsening dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) and are opened by endoscopic dilation (balloon stretching of the join).

steps.say: Every bypass creates two gaps in the mesentery, and bowel can slide through either of them. The Petersen gap sits between the food limb and the transverse colon drape and the second sits at the foot join, and both are stitched shut with permanent suture. Hernias peak after major weight loss paradoxically, because melting internal fat opens the gaps wider.
steps.tx: Two mesenteric gaps threaten every bypass: the **Petersen defect** (space between the food-limb mesentery and the transverse mesocolon) and the jejunojejunal window. Both are stitched shut with permanent nonabsorbable suture during the primary operation. **Internal hernia** (bowel trapped in a reopened gap) clusters after major weight loss, when melting fat slackens the closure. Colicky pain with swirling bowel on CT means urgent operation.

steps.say: Supplements after bariatric surgery are for life, not for a season. Every patient takes multivitamins with calcium, vitamin D, B12, iron and thiamine, while bypass patients add copper and zinc. Skipping them leads to anaemia, burning feet from neuropathy, and Wernicke confusion from thiamine lack. Bloods are checked every 6 to 12 months without fail.
steps.tx: **Lifelong supplementation** (vitamins and minerals forever after surgery) with multivitamins plus calcium, vitamin D, **B12**, iron and **thiamine** (vitamin B1) follows all bariatric procedures, with copper and zinc added after bypass. Gaps cause anaemia (low haemoglobin), neuropathy (nerve damage) and **Wernicke** disease (thiamine-deficiency confusion), so bloods are checked every **6 to 12** months.

steps.say: Dumping comes in two waves after bypass and sleeve surgery. The early wave hits within 30 minutes of sweet food with flushing, palpitations and diarrhoea. The late wave arrives at 1 to 3 hours as sweating and shakiness from excess insulin. Small low sugar meals with fluids kept separate from solids control most cases without further surgery.
steps.tx: Early **dumping syndrome** (sugars rushing into the bowel) provokes sweating, palpitations and diarrhoea inside **30** minutes of a sweet meal, while **late hypoglycaemia** (insulin overshoot) brings shakiness at **1 to 3** hours. Small low-glycaemic portions with drinks kept apart from solids control most sufferers, leaving revision surgery a rarity.
